#388. Building AI that can work across the enterprise

Moving AI beyond isolated pilots requires a strong data foundation, clear business outcomes, and governance built for enterprise scale.

For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model.

For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.”

That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can't scale is just an experiment,” he says.

Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn't speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit.

Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond.

This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys.

Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I'm Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.

This episode is produced in partnership with Infosys.Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we're still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI's value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It's becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can't simply be added into an enterprise's existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what's inside and how it's used.

Two words for you: conscious configuration.My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy.Welcome, Thorsten and Satinder.

Thorsten Leiduck: Yeah, thank you for having us. Really a pleasure to be here with our valued partner, Infosys. Looking forward to the conversation.

Satinder Pal Singh: Hi, Megan. Thanks for inviting for the conversation today. Looking forward to the discussion.

Megan: Me too. Thank you both so much for being here. Thorsten, if I could start with you. We know that many senior leaders understand the transformative potential in AI, but they continue to struggle with aspects of its implementation. Many projects remain stuck at a pilot phase, for example. When you speak to clients, what are the biggest obstacles they face when it comes to integrating AI into their tech stack?

Thorsten: Yeah. Megan, as you mentioned, AI is on the agenda of every client conversation today, but many customers are really struggling how to convert that interest into an operationalized model and to unlock the value of AI across the enterprise. And the reason is that too many programs start as isolated POCs on different AI technologies and in an inconsistent fragmented data foundation.This creates a lot of duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale. At the same time, leaders are highly concerned about security, observability, reliability of agents, and some ethical implications when those get deployed. This is also shown in some studies. For example, BCG has launched a report, which shows that 74% of the organizations are stuck in pilot mode with no plan to scale. And in an Anthropic survey, data said that 42% are really struggling with getting access to the data and the quality to really, basically, scale the entire AI capabilities across the organization.The path forward is really to treat AI not just as a project, but more holistically, as an enterprise platform, one that really consistently connects an unified data layer with the process context of the applications, and then embed AI capabilities governed across the entire life cycle. And to make this real, we in SAP launched the SAP autonomous enterprise framework, so organizations can move from pilots to scaled outcomes.

Megan: Yeah, really, to provide that support. And, Satinder, would you agree, why is it that we're seeing enterprises get a touch of almost AI paralysis here? What's the mindset shift that needs to happen and, perhaps, why is this something organizations need to be thinking about now, as well?

Satinder: Absolutely, Megan. And, if anything, the picture sharpens when you look at, specifically, at agentic AI. Infosys and HFS research surveyed over 500 global 2,000 enterprises and found only 14% have successfully scaled AI. Eighty-six percent remain in early exploration, proof of concept, or fragmented pilot phases. For a technology at the top of every boardroom agenda for two years, that's a striking failure rate. And at the core of that 86% is what I would describe as AI as a department trap.

What happens is that an organization creates an AI team or a center of excellence and walls it off from business. That team builds technically excellent pilots the business doesn't recognize itself in, and you end up with AI solutions searching for problems, rather than the other way around. Mindset shift is clear. Move from treating AI as a technology initiative to treating it as an operating model transformation. AI stops being something IT does for business and starts being something the whole organization does together. Every function, every workflow, embedded from the start.

And what makes this a now problem? Early movers are building an advantage. You cannot close by buying the same platform later. Eighteen months of agent behavior data, calibrated knowledge graph, workforce that has genuinely internalized AI, that is a structural advantage that compounds. Infosys Knowledge Institute AI Maturity Index shows that only 8% of the companies qualify as AI native today, yet they achieve four times the revenue contribution from the AI versus laggards. If you're not building AI today, you're not standing still, you're falling behind at an accelerating rate.

Megan: Right. There's a real polarization there, isn't there, between the front-runners and the laggards, as you say. As we shift from pilot to scaled-up applications, perhaps the first step is evaluating when AI is the right tool. AI has quickly become the default solution within many enterprises. Is there a tendency to use it as a bit of a blunt instrument, nowadays, Thorsten? At the outset, how can senior leaders better evaluate what use cases are worthy of their time and investment, in order to strip out some of that later complexity?

Thorsten: Yeah, I think, Megan, what everybody needs to be aware is adopting and rolling out AI across an organization is as much a change management journey as it's a technology rollout.Now, when you have this in mind, it makes absolutely sense to put AI in front as many teams as possible, because you want to build formality, and spark ideas, and also people should see the benefit of AI in an organization. When you think about travel assistance, meeting summaries via Copilot, or AI-enabled workflows, increase the productivity, everybody feels this in their real job, in their real daily business. And, obviously, this creates creativity and also provides the organization from a bottom-up perspective with some innovation scale.

Now, however, as majority grows, the conversation, and this is also what we discuss with many of the leaders, and our clients, shifts more to economics and governance. Things like token costs, model performance, security, and accountability become much more relevant. And when you then take the approach and think about AI agents as digital workers that execute specific tasks within a business process, then this means, from an AI perspective, not every task justifies nation.

In some cases, human effort remains more economical or effective. The smart approach, and that's what we really recommend to our clients, is to start with a defined, maybe small set of high-value use cases with defined success metrics upfront. So, for example, such as cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, or cost of per transaction, or top line improvement, and then scale what works. Those use cases can be tied to a line of business domains or industry scenarios.

And then, what we are doing from an SAP perspective, together with Infosys, we really help customers to be successful. We provide, as part of our autonomous suite, the according domain assistance, which really run business processes end-to-end and which deliver find ROIs for single end-to-end business process steps.

And then, last but not least, in many scenarios, I think, which has been very common pattern in particular around large industry AI use cases, is a joint approach, and we do this with partners like Infosys, but also customers around forward deployed engineering, so that you really define very closely the AI-specific use case with the defined outcomes together with the customer, and deliver this as the initial projects. And then, ideally, scale this to other customers and take it back like a best practice, which can be rolled out to other organizations, as well.

Megan: Right. It's been really clear, isn't it, on what you're looking to achieve and what's worth your time, as I say. And what would your advice, Satinder, be here, on refining an AI strategy to ensure organizations can focus on those areas, where AI can deliver the highest returns?

Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten's framing of AI agents as digital coworkers forces a precision that agentic AI strategy language often lacks. When you ask which digital coworkers do we need and where do they deliver the most value, the answer starts to become clearer right from the first step. At Infosys, through our Topaz AI-first framework, we push clients through the three lenses simultaneously.The first one is impact. Where does deploying an agent move the numbers that matter? Revenue, cost, working capital risk. We have built a library of over 300 enterprise use cases across industries, so we never begin from a blank page. The second is feasibility. Given your data foundation platform and talent today, which high-impact use cases can you actually execute? Feasibility determines your sequence. The high-impact use case on a broken data foundation is not viable. When the foundation is right, the results are dramatic. One Infosys engagement cut complex SAP-specification documents from 86 person hours to 6, a 92% reduction.Third is scalability. Once you have proven a use case with clear ROI metrics, cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, cost per transaction, what's the architecture that lets you replicate it? A pilot that can't scale is just an experiment. My practical advice: treat your AI portfolio like an investment portfolio, quick wins that fund the program, medium-term bets, one or two bold, long-term positions that balance keep stakeholders engaged at every stage and not just in year three.

Megan: That's such a useful framework for people to use there. And given the urgency here, Thorsten, how can organizations approach and manage AI in a more structured, efficient way? To start with, what are the fundamentals that some organizations perhaps miss at the moment? I know Infosys and SAP talk about platform and data, then AI, for example.

Thorsten: Yeah, Megan, I think the fundamental, which many organizations are overlooking, is data and the data is a foundation for AI. Because, at the end, without the data structures and the ability to access the right information at the right time and basically bringing different kind of structured, unstructured data sources together, in a meaningful governed and semantic way, there will be no successful AI. AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation. And I think this is often overlooked, and that's why I said when you start POCs in different organization, or different parts of the organization with different technologies, it's very hard to establish an end-to-end consistent model on the data side, as well as on the AI side.

One of the key goals companies need to achieve is, and that's why we really talk about you need to start with data first and the platform first, is to establish and semantically-rich connected data layer that really reflects your business, so that the agents are really grounded in the company's reality and not just in generic patterns.

And then, I think, the second element that's important is accuracy. In the enterprise context, it really matters. For example, what might pass in a consumer setting, where you have 80% accuracy, and even in a workforce environment where you build PowerPoints or you do email drafts, which you then, with a human in the loop, optimize, 80% might be good enough. But, when you really think about mission-critical or business-critical processes in the supply chain, or closing the books, 80% is a very terrible result.

The stakes are much too high and you need to have much more accuracy. And that's why it's important that you have business process logic and industry context embedded into the data and the models which build the foundation, if you will, the backbone for every AI and, obviously, for the data in the ERP and the line of business system.

And then, last but not least, the other critical element, and you see this obviously in the news with all the agents going rogue, are governance, compliance, and security. Very critical in an enterprise context. You need to set clear policies, access controls. You need to have monitoring ability, capabilities, to really make sure that what then the AI agenda capabilities or agents are executing is fully aligned, is trustworthy, and scalable.

Megan: Right. Which is quite a lot of things for organizations to be thinking about. Satinder, how do SAP and Infosys work with organizations to streamline some of these processes, perhaps and make unlocking AI's capability a little bit easier?

Satinder: Megan, I think at the onset, I want to acknowledge that, at Infosys, we are uniquely positioned for our relationship with SAP, because we are a customer to SAP, as well as one of their key global suppliers. And the way SAP and Infosys work together is designed around the architecture Thorsten described, that defines a coherent partnership.

SAP brings the platform foundation, business data cloud for the semantically-rich enterprise, generative AI hub for governed LLMXs, and agent hub for the lifecycle governance, enterprise grade from day one. Infosys brings implementation depth, industry context, and use case accelerators. Through Infosys Topaz, we have built over 50 pre-configured AI use cases on Business AI Platform, production-ready configurations deployable without building from scratch. We co-develop use cases within SAP's industry AI engagement with clear customer-specific FTE metrics. That shared accountability for results is different from a typical implementation engagement.

In practice, one global S/4HANA transformation program used AI-assisted delivery tooling to complete over 480 RICEF objects in five months, a pace conventional delivery would not sustain. In another account, an AI-powered platform auto-classifies over 120,000 SAP incidents monthly, with zero analyst charge. The combined effect time to value drops from 12 to 18 months, down to four to six months.

What I would emphasize is change management damage. Technology is increasingly deployable, and Thorsten also spoke about it earlier. What's hard is helping an organization internalize that their agents are digital coworkers, not automations. That mindset shift is 70% of the implementation challenge that platform cannot solve alone, and Infosys and SAP run joint adoption programs addressing both the dimensions in parallel.

Megan: Fantastic. Some great real-world examples there, as well. Thorsten, can you tell us a little bit more about SAP's Business AI Platform, or BAIP, in particular? How does that work and what sets it apart from other platforms?

Thorsten: Yeah, so SAP Business AI Platform, if you will, is the foundation for our SAP autonomous enterprise framework, which really consists of a unified user interface and is enabled as an agentic orchestration layer, which we call Joule. And you have the autonomous read with all the applications, and then you have the Business AI Platform, which powers the other capabilities, and is closely connected, and is basically organized around three core pillars.

The first one is, really, what we call build. What it means is you provide the respective intent-based development tools, so that customer, or partners like Infosys, can really create and development agents, applications and workflows using best-in-class tools and model to extend SAP's own assistant, or customizing those, or really building own agents as needed.

Complimenting what Satinder said, it's really critical for us that we have a thriving ecosystem, who is innovative, and is building innovations, and is complementing our own SAP agentic portfolio. We are focusing on specific areas on the domains, from a line of business industry perspective, where we deliver assistance as part of our organization, but to really then customize them from a last mile execution from really complimenting areas which we don't cover and really driving the innovation towards the customer, our ecosystem is the multiplier force and Infosys is really playing a leading role here with us, together.

Second is, and we talked about this, is what we call the contextualize and reason pillar, which is literally as a foundation data, we address with SAP Data Cloud and comprehensive data strategy, where we establish an end-to-end data fabric across partner provider platforms, like Databricks, Snowflakes, where we promote and zero copy access to data. For the customer, this is very important. So, we allow, basically, promote to customers if you have made investments in any of those platforms, reserve those investments and just leverage BDC to connect without moving data around your, for example, Databricks, Snowflake environment to BDC.

With this approach, we establish and harmonize semantic data layer, which can then be used for any AI scenario across the entire enterprise, combining different data sources without any disruption. The other key element that's part of this is the generative AI hub. We have aggregated more than 50 models, language models, including some of our own models into it, in single cockpit, so that customers can access and choose any of those 50 models as part of the generative-AI hub, which is part of the platform.

And then, as a key differentiator, we really moved a lot of business semantic and context into the knowledge graph, which then helps to navigate the agents and acts like a nerve, or navigation system, in the company to really provide business-relevant, customer-specific information for the decision making and the execution to any agentic execution framework.

And then, we talked about governance, last but not least. This is the third pillar, which is very critical and this is built-in. So, we have, as the third pillar, the SAP agent hub, which is kind of a command center for enterprise-wide AI and agent governments. You can govern SAP agents, you can also govern non-SAP agents, as long as they're integrating to SAP via A2A. So, the team can really manage, on the customer side, an end-to-end life cycle of agents and features from hire to retire.

Megan: Fantastic. That's a really comprehensive overview. Thank you ever so much. And, Satinder, can you share any examples, perhaps, of how organizations have used SAP Business AI Platform in practice, to improve the ways they've used AI? Perhaps, what was the challenge they faced, what did the process look like, and what benefits did they unlock?

Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten just explained how powerful a platform Business AI Platform is. And this is decades in working. We also have been using that, and I'll share two examples from live Infosys engagements, both showing what BIP's three pillar look like in production.

The first is global diversified manufacturer with a large SAP estate. The challenge was month-end close, 80-plus SAP transaction codes, period closed teams working nights and weekends, L1 support absorbing over 300 incidents per month, from close cycle alone. On Business AI Platform, we deployed Topaz Fabric, Infosys' agentic orchestration platform, with a master agent coordinating five specialist child agents, WBS accrual, revenue recognition, intercompany settlement, master data reconciliation, and SOX audit trail generation. Agents run autonomously, escalating to humans only for genuine exceptions. The result, entire L1.5 support tier eliminated, over 300 monthly incidents handled with zero human touch. The close team redeployed from reactive firefighting to forward-looking financial analysis. Annual savings pipeline exceed $1 million.The second is North American Utility in a S/4HANA transformation. Their challenge was development velocity, complex SAP functional specification documents routinely requiring 80 or more personnel each, a bottleneck throttling the entire program. Using AI native development environment on Business AI Platform with a Claude-powered retrieval system, we reduced those specifications from 86 hours to six, a 92% reduction, validated across 51 SAP task types at 95% accuracy. The architecture is now being replicated across accounts. In both cases, the pattern matches what Thorsten described, governed data foundation, SAP business process context, full agent observability through SAP Agent Hub. That's the autonomous enterprise running as daily operations, not as a concept.

Megan: And those are some really compelling concrete results I think would be really helpful for people to hear. Also, of course, responsible AI, or clear governance frameworks, are a critical component of AI integration, too. And we know that tools like LLMs are rarely developed with compliance built-in. I wonder what's your advice there, Thorsten, on how to ensure that property governance is embedded into an ERP?

Thorsten: Yeah, I mean, Megan, you're absolutely right. Governance compliance and security are really mission-critical to delivering relevant, reliable, and trustworthy AI at enterprise scale. I mean, it's important to understand how in public LLM service really works. Many of those services are trained on internet scale data, which means they're public models. Depending on the provider's policies and setting, they may retain easier inputs for model improvement, which means if a company provides data back to the model, this company data is in the public domain. For example, pipeline information or forecast information, which is becoming very, very critical, because this exposes your organization, really, at significant risk.

So, while then LLMs X are really great, imposes in large volumes of text and other unstructured data, they are less effective with structured tables like in EOP systems, or in business applications, in general, and then they're lacking, usually, the nuance of business process and logic and context. That's why a robust governance framework is essential. We talked about the generative AI, how we aggregate those models in a single cockpit.

And then, the other element, which we previously touched based on and Satinder mentioned, is always a part of the custom examples is SAP agent hub or, in general, when we talk about the capabilities just in AI lifecycle governance, which really includes agent registry, LMN registries, MCP registry, so a single source of tool for every AI artifact that you can manage identity and access control, so that agents are really variable and that you can really provide the right permissions, in terms of which agents allowed to use access which data, and then agent observability, agent minus, and then also map the agent skills to the organization is very critical.

As all of part of this, as I mentioned before, we provide those capabilities really fully embedded into the Business AI Platform to really provide this governance framework out of the box and fully embedded into everything what you do at SAP.

Megan: Which is so important, because when organizations are experimenting with, or scaling up multiple AI programs and tools, in some cases, it adds real complexity. I wonder, Satinder, would you add anything on how organizations can have that robust layer of governance built in, even with a pretty complex tech stack?

Satinder: We, at Infosys, have our Infosys Knowledge Institute, they run this annual magazine generative AI radar, and it found that 48% of companies had deployed generative AI without a formal governance policy. Nearly half of the enterprises were running AI with no documented framework or oversight, accountability, or compliance. That's the gap that Thorsten is describing, and it has to be closed proactively before an incident forces a reactive stop or audit far more disruptive than building a governance upfront.What Thorsten has just described in SAP Agent Hub is exactly the platform layer that makes enterprise-wide governance possible and is worth making the overall architecture explicit, because without it, governance is theoretical.The framework I use with clients has three layers that have to work together. The first one is policy, a clear organization-wide AI use policy, what agents can and cannot do autonomously, how data can be used for AI training, disclosure obligations, and accountability for outcomes. This needs legal, compliance, technology teams together with a board level sponsorship. Without that foundation, every deployment becomes an ad hoc governance debate. Second layer is platform. This is where SAP Business AI Platform and, specifically, SAP Agent Hub becomes enterprise control tower.The capabilities Thorsten described, agent LLM, MCP registry as a single source of truth, verifiable agent identities with scoped access trails, agent observability, agent mining for drift detection, these aren't just governance features. They give leaders real-time visibility across a complex multi-agent landscape. You can see what's running, what it's consuming, and whether it's performing as expected. That's what turns a complex tech stack from a governance liability to a governance asset.

And the last layer is process, the recurring governance rituals, quarterly AI risk reviews, bias audit cycles, model performance reviews against the business KPIs, these structured conversations that keep humans accountable for the agent behavior over time. What organizations consistently discover is that this three-layer structure actually accelerates the deployment. Every new use case has a clear path through approval and a governance architecture to plug into. The absence of governance doesn't speed up AI adoption. It creates a risk backlog that eventually forces a stop and audit movement far more disruptive than building the governance muscle.

Megan: That's such an interesting point. Thank you so much for that. And we've covered a lot of ground, so to close with a future forward look, we've spoken today about the proliferation of AI tools that are now on the market, many designed to transform enterprise-level operations. I wonder, what do you see on the horizon, Thorsten, that you think could be a real game-changer?

Thorsten: I think what we will see very soon, and we talked about this briefly, is that we are heading into a period of sustained, rapid AI adoption, where assistance and agents will operate as digital coworkers. They will be embedded in our organizations like employees today, and they will be embedded into processes as people perform tasks, as we speak.Now, as this happens, the Center of Gravity will shift more and more from a monolithic application layer to an agentic value layer that orchestrates work across systems and across different landscapes, which need to be orchestrated very well. I think what we also will see, and this will be likely, at least in terms of scale, I believe a game-changer, is that the delivery will become industrialized. When you think about agent factories and church services that really design, test, and govern agents at scale, or you can say agentic frameworks at scale, and I think we will see an evolution of commercial models, which are today more consumption-based towards really value and outcome-based agreements, which are then tied to clear business KPIs.On the technology front, I think there's still so much movement on the LLM landscape, new architectures, training methods. I think we'll bring down, significantly, the total cost of ownership, while also control and the viability will be improved. I think there's an awareness which the recent examples in the market show, and then I think the innovation will be playable.And I think the big question is, from that perspective, which role is China going to play in a global context, and also how those models are really embedded. Last but not least, most importantly, even I think ontology and customer-specific knowledge graphs will become first-class assets, and I think this will be the key differentiation in the future, because they will lead in code process, semantics, policies, what Satinder talked about, and data relationships. And they are the blueprint for secure high-performing enterprise agent architectures in the future.

Megan: Which is, of course, what we're aiming for. And how about you, Satinder? What would you flag as a really exciting area of development?

Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think what excites me most is the shift from AI as productivity tool to AI as a decision-making partner. The most important evolution Thorsten's architecture makes possible. For decades, enterprise systems have told us what happened. The next generation helps leader understand what is happening now, what will happen next, what actions to take.

The scenario I keep coming back to, a CFO starting a day with an agent that continuously analyzes signals across finance, supply chain, procurement, workforce data, proactively surfacing the three issues that are most likely to impact the quarter, with recommended actions, financial impact quantified. That's not a dashboard. That's a fundamentally different decision model. Through Infosys Topaz, we are helping clients move forward an AI-first enterprise, one that can sense, learn, decide, adapt continuously across the different domains.

What also excites me is the pace of AI evolution. In past technology waves, constraints were stable. You identify a limitation and architect around it for years. AI is different. Use cases that appear constrained at program start are often resolved before go live. SAP's prior model transformed structured data reasoning once a clear LLM gap. Decision intelligence is arriving faster than most organization are planning for.

The winning strategy is to design for where AI will be 18 months from now, flexible architecture, trusted data foundation, governance that absorbs innovation as it arrives. Organizations that do this compound value at each new generation of capabilities becomes available.

So, the next frontier isn't that AI can do more work. It's that AI that understands your business well enough to help you make better decision. And that's where the greatest opportunity for SAP, Infosys, and our clients lies, convergence of systems of record with systems of intelligence.

Megan: Fantastic. Certainly, lots on the horizon to look forward to. Thank you both so much for joining us today.That was Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America at SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England.

#382. Nike lays out financial goals ahead of first investor day in 9 years

Nike said Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance.

The retailer also laid out a financial framework and said that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50. The company said higher-quality revenue, gross margin expansion and productivity improvements would help it reach its goals.

Nike's 2027 financial guidance includes expectations for revenue to decline in the high-single-digit range, an adjusted operating margin of approximately 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35.

The company also introduced a strategy it's calling Full Stride Ahead, which the company said aims "to get closer to athletes and focus resources on the greatest opportunities for long-term growth."

"We're concentrating our resources where we have the greatest potential to win," Nike CEO Elliott Hill said in a statement. "We're also changing how we operate — delivering breakthrough products, building deeper local connections and moving faster to capture demand. Together, these actions are designed to return NIKE to sustainable, profitable growth."

Nike said it would focus on performance sports and sportswear opportunities "with the greatest potential for long-term growth," and said its five priority sports would be running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor.

Nike is holding an investor day at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the company aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump.

Last month, the company reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it announced a restructuring plan, including layoffs that it said would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year.

Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the company said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027.

The new strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the company's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike said the turnaround plan is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031.

Nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have said the company is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers.

At the same time, Nike announced last quarter that it's creating a new global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company said it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence.

CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has said that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the company elsewhere, including internationally.

The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises.

Shares of Nike have fallen 50% over the past two years.

#381. Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 17, 2026

The Moon has reached its First Quarter phase, with half of its visible surface now illuminated. Over the coming days, the Moon will keep getting bigger a we move towards the Full Moon.

As of Tuesday, Nov. 17, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the First Quarter phase, with 48% of its surface visible.

If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Vaporum, Fecunditatis, and Crisium. With binoculars, you'll also see the Endymion Crater, Posidonius Crater, and the Mare Nectaris. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 17 landing spot and the Linne Crater.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

According to NASA, the Moon goes through a complete cycle of phases roughly every 29.5 days. As it orbits Earth, the portion of its sunlit surface visible to us changes, giving rise to the different lunar phases. The cycle begins with a New Moon, progresses to a Full Moon, and then gradually returns to a New Moon before starting all over again.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

#379. Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it

While we’re used to predictable technology, AI challenges that assumption. Therefore, the goal must be bounded, observable, and controllable AI.

In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.

For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.

AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.

We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.

Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.

Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.

With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.

Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.

It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.

Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.

The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.

Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:

The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

#375. The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back

Supporters are signing a petition to reinstate Huang. But findings on Nvidia chips in China and a new Commerce rule are threatening open-source AI’s reputation and progress regardless.

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.

But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.

But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

#373. Oobah Butler Can Sell You Anything—If You’re a Rich Idiot

You’d think that Oobah Butler would have run out of schemes by now.

The gonzo British documentarian’s repertoire includes creating an entirely fake restaurant—The Shed at Dulwich—and getting it to the top spot on London’s Tripadvisor; selling bottles of Amazon drivers’ urine on the ecommerce site; and convincing venture capitalists to give him $1 million.

But as his new HBO show, Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow, makes perfectly clear, Butler still has plenty of tricks up his sleeve—and it’s a delight to watch them unfold.

The series launches November 22. Each of the premier season’s five episodes centers on Butler scamming his way into success in a different industry—wellness, wine, dating, music, and a finale I do not want to spoil—with increasingly outlandish ideas that, somehow, almost no one advises him against.

His shock of bleach-blond hair and appearance of a Victorian ghost notwithstanding, there are undeniable similarities between Butler’s style and that of master of manipulation Nathan Fielder. Both use satire and parody to make social commentaries, and both often divert from their original plans by hyperfocusing on what the average person might consider a tangential detail, carrying these side quests to extreme lengths. But while Fielder has sometimes been criticized for roping unassuming working-class folks into his hijinks, in Butler’s case the joke is almost always on the rich and powerful—and the systems that allow them to prevail.

“The whole show can be reduced to ‘monkey see, monkey do,’” Butler tells me from a coffee shop at the New York Historical Society in Manhattan, where he’s just ordered a latte with four espresso shots and been recognized from TikTok by a fellow patron. “I just find these bad actors and copy them.”

Butler’s knack for convincing high-profile—in some cases notorious—executives and tastemakers to appear on camera and earnestly weigh in on his ridiculous plans at times boggles the mind. In the series premiere, he sets out to start a wellness company that sells the tears of human children as a skin serum, and gets none other than former Theranos chief creative officer Patrick O’Neill to consult on a marketing strategy.

Applying his characteristic charm, Butler tells O’Neill he “smashed it” with creating mystique around the scandal-plagued biotech startup, to which O’Neill replies, “Thank you, yeah. I think it’s good to share the knowledge.”

Butler wearing glasses designed to collect the tears of children.

After briefly expressing hesitancy around the ethical sourcing of the tears, O’Neill begins offering Butler packaging advice: a tear-shaped bottle, and the two discuss the name Lacrimé (“tears” in Italian). “It makes it feel exotic and not necessarily something you’d see from Johnson and Johnson,” O’Neill says, in all seriousness.

Confiding in $1,500-an-hour lawyer Jennifer Keller about how he may have committed fraud with his wellness venture, Butler tells her the industry is “a gold rush of bullshit. And I want in.” She laughs and says that he sounds “more and more like an American.” It’s all very funny, but as the name of the show hints, there is a Robin Hood quality to Butler’s scamming, in this case exposing the poorly regulated nature of skin care and supplements.

Butler has chosen the New York Historical Society as our meeting point because he loves history, and New York’s in particular. When he first moved here in February 2024, he started reading Robert Caro’s The Power Broker, a biography of influential urban planner Robert Moses, giving him an understanding of “how power works” in the city. But his itch to move came well before that, when he visited in 2016.

“I just found it so inspiring,” he says, dressed in a maroon velvet shirt, baggy dark jeans, and Salomon sneakers, a Patagonia backpack slung over his shoulders, as we set out for a walk in Central Park. “I got to an age where I just thought, well if I don’t do this now, I probably am not going to do it.”

Although New York is indeed full of power brokers—and very wealthy ones at that—he says it’s different from the aristocracy he grew up around in Feckenham, a 700-person “Hobbiton-style village” in the UK.

“I grew up in a lower-class family … I’ve definitely got a bit of a chip on my shoulder about class,” he says, noting that he’s the youngest of six siblings. “And America, for all of its issues, there is something amazing about how I see the same guys who really wind me up in the UK—upper-class kind of guys—and the way that they walk the earth and the way they feel and the way they carry themselves. I see them come here and no one gives a shit. Really, truly, no one gives a shit.”

Butler didn't go to college. He started a band called My Grey Horse in 2010, playing guitar and singing. Around the age of 17, he began writing music reviews, secretly hoping to score his band some coverage. “It was a scam on the go,” he says. But he caught the writing bug, finding it “meditative.” Later, he joined VICE (where I previously worked as a senior reporter) as a freelance video host, making a bunch of documentaries, including the extremely viral one about The Shed. From there, he did several films for the UK’s Channel 4 and cohosted MTV’s Catfish UK.

“It changed my life and was absolutely the right thing to do. I wouldn't have been able to afford to move here if I hadn't done Catfish,” he says.

Though he tells me he’s not a comedian, Butler is a natural clown, and at times even just his buffoonish mannerisms are enough to elicit laughs. Maybe he’s such a natural because he comes from a long line of schemers. He tells me his great grandfather moved to the US in the late 19th century as part of the fur trade, but he would also sell rabbit droppings rolled in flour as medicine.

“I'm cut from a line of people who sell shit,” he says.

Though he may not have firsthand experiences, Butler’s perceptions of hoity-toity cultural institutions—and their vulnerabilities—are spot on. In an episode about fine wine, he embarks on a mission to sell a smoke-tainted swill brand called Fumare as a high-end product—even though it would normally be tossed by wine producers or used for barbecue sauces. Part of his task is to convince New York Times wine critic Eric Asimov to give the smoked wine a good review.

Butler creates a psychological profile of Asimov, determining that he’s a “contrarian” who “wants to be romanced.” Knowing he’s a fan of Bob Dylan, Butler just happens to be playing a Dylan song on the piano when Asimov shows up for a tasting. While Asimov pans the first glass of smoky wine, Butler tries again, by pretending it's actually a glass of Barolo, the same stuff Asimov says he fell in love with when he first got into wine. “I have no complaints,” Asimov says—an endorsement that Butler promptly attaches to Fumare’s label.

In another episode, Butler starts an AI dating company called Sole, but instead of matching people with a chatbot, as he’s purporting to do, he matches them with other humans to see if they connect.

“The idea was that people trust in the technology more than a conversation with one another,” he says.

These days, many of Butler’s stunts either directly or indirectly relate to Big Tech—for good reason.

“A lot of it is built on speculative promises and the idea of utopia rather than connected to reality. Tech CEOs constantly coming out and lying about what they’ll be able to do in 10 years to shit-coin their stock price,” he says, adding that the sector is “riddled with inauthenticity.”

Despite having the backing of HBO, his own work still feels authentic and haphazard, as opposed to overly polished. He says it’s usually just him and a couple of other people carrying out the stunts. “One of the episodes was basically me and me in my bedroom,” he says, noting that while he’s been working on the finale for six years, originally envisioning it as a feature film, all the others except for the pilot were shot in the last eight months.

“There’s a DIY characteristic to the stuff anyway, and I want the people watching to not feel excluded from the pieces of it. And that's always a thing where I'm like, ‘Oh, if the budget for the show was much bigger, it might not feel like this anymore,’” he tells me.

Considering all the pranks he’s pulled off, I ask him point-blank if it’s a bad idea for people to answer the phone when he calls. He rebuffs, pressing me for my take.

Truthfully, I think there’s a high chance that if you engage with Butler on camera, you’ll come off looking like a fool—particularly if you’re someone with any type of clout. But for the sake of my own entertainment, I hope people keep doing it.

#370. Republicans outspent Democrats for first time in over a decade in record 2026 midterm election political ad blitz

Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence company AdImpact released Tuesday.

Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.

The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.

Despite Republicans leading spending, John Link, senior vice president of data at AdImpact, said that "Dems still led or were generally even with overall airings and impressions."

The record spending extended across the board, with every type of race reaching a new high. Senate spending hit $3.39 billion, while spending on gubernatorial elections reached $2.61 billion, spending on races in the House of Representatives grew to $2.44 billion and state legislative races totaled $602 million, all records, according to AdImpact.

The 2026 midterm cycle was largely powered by megadonors, with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk becoming the largest contributor by funneling more than $366 million into campaigns.

The biggest donors in this year's election disproportionately favored Republicans, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records. Fourteen out of the 20 largest donor groups supported GOP candidates, according to that analysis.

Republicans spent $5.51 billion on political advertisements, compared with $5.11 billion spent by Democrats, according to AdImpact.

While Republican spending increased by 27% from 2024, spending by Democrats fell by 4%.

Fundraisers told CNBC in interviews that Democratic donors' hesitancy largely stems from memories of Kamala Harris' defeat in 2024, unease about the rise of democratic socialism and distrust in party leadership.

Though they were outspent, Democrats made sweeping gains against Republicans in races nationwide, taking control of both the House and the Senate and flipping seats in some of the most competitive places, including Texas and Kansas.

It is not the first time spending did not align with the winners. In 2024, President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Harris despite Democrats outspending Republicans.

While party majorities in Congress have switched hands, the most popular medium for political ads has not changed.

Broadcast television represented the largest category for spending in this year's election, accounting for 49%, or $5.85 billion, of political ad spending, according to AdImpact. Broadcast's share of political ad dollars is up slightly from 48% in 2024.

Broadcast TV's strength comes despite facing pressure from falling viewership and increasing competition from streaming.

Industry experts have told CNBC that political advertisers continue to spend on broadcast because it reaches local markets and active voting populations. The Associated Press also reported that airtime was so expensive during the midterm elections that some candidates, including Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, bought ads during national sporting events, figuring that reaching enough constituents through a national broadcast might actually be less expensive than buying across the state's local television markets.

The fastest-growing categories in this year's cycle were connected TV, or internet-connected devices like Apple TV or Roku, with $2.66 billion, and digital, with $1.91 billion. Both mediums grew double digits from the 2024 presidential election. Spending on cable and radio declined 7% and 13%, respectively, from 2024.

#369. GTA 6 New Zealand time trick for Xbox, PS5: How to play hours early

GTA fans have waited 13 years for Grand Theft Auto VI. Finally, the next installment of the GTA series comes out on Nov. 19.

There's no early access for GTA 6. In theory, you have to wait until the release date. But what if you could play GTA 6 on Nov. 18? Or, more accurately, roughly 18 hours before everyone else in the U.S.? Well, there's a way to do just that.

GTA 6 will have a global release date, dropping at midnight for each time zone. This means that New Zealand, which is 18 hours ahead of Eastern Time in the U.S., will get to play the long-awaited game before everyone else.

If you have an Xbox, there's long been a not-so-secret trick on Xbox consoles that lets U.S.-based gamers access games a little bit before everyone else in the country.

As our friends at PCMag point out, gamers can simply go to their Xbox dashboard and do the following:

Select Language & Location on the right-hand side

Hit Restart Now to restart your console and save the settings

This has previously worked to access other games early, as it tricks the console into thinking it's on New Zealand time. It's possible that Microsoft switches things up and closes the loophole before the launch of GTA 6. But, as of now, unless anything changes, it should work.

This is a quick and easy process, and you'll be able to change the settings back on your Xbox the same way.

Also, be sure to preorder the digital version of GTA 6 as you'll be able to download the game on Nov. 10. While it won't be playable until the release, it'll be ready to go on your console as soon as it does release without having to wait for the game to download and install then.

PlayStation 5 users, unfortunately, don't have it so simple. And there's no guarantee that this will work either. So, before we go any further, know that it just might not be worth the time and effort.

PlayStation accounts are region-locked, so Sony knows exactly where you're based when you're signed into your account.

If you want to attempt to access GTA 6 early on your PS5, create a new PSN account while using a VPN (we recommend ExpressVPN) with a New Zealand-based location. From there, you'll actually have to purchase the game under this new account in the New Zealand PlayStation Store. As PCMag points out, this might even cost more due to currency conversions.

And, again, there is no guarantee that this will work.

Worst case, you have to wait another 18 hours before you can play a game you've already waited 13 years for.

#368. Are Smart Car Seats Worth It? I Tested Two to Find Out (2026)

Car seats had some pretty humble beginnings. Even I, an early-’90s baby, slightly recoil every time I see a picture of myself strapped into a flimsy plastic bucket with a loud geometric-print cover that once held my life in its clutches. Car seat design and safety standards have come a long way, and today’s models are quite souped up, with cup holders, rotating bases, and enough bells and whistles to rival an Escalade. And now, they’re getting smart.

Many car seat manufacturers are adding technology to, for lack of a better term, give parents a second set of eyes. Think Bluetooth-connected chest clips, sensors, apps, and real-time alerts that ping your phone if something goes awry, whether that’s an installation issue or if a chest clip comes unbuckled while the car’s moving.

It sounds appealing, right? Especially for parents who already have plenty to worry about and are often juggling a million things just to get out the door in the morning. But it’s worth asking: Do these features actually make car seats safer? Or are parents paying for peace of mind?

I tested two smart car seats, the Babyark Classic ($799) and the Cybex Cloud G Pro ($550), to see if this technology lives up to the hype and whether a smart seat is worth adding to your registry. Because while an app-connected car seat might seem cool and offer some reassurance, no amount of technology can replace proper installation and use. Keep in mind that they’re not exactly apples-to-apples comparisons; the Babyark is a convertible car seat designed to grow with your little one, while the Cybex is an infant carrier. I tested the Babyark with my toddler daughter and the Cybex with my infant son, giving me a chance to see how each one worked at different stages of parenthood. But both offer a glimpse into how companies are integrating technology into car seats, and I wanted to see how they perform in everyday life.

Many smart car seats revolve around sensors. Some come equipped with sensors that help caregivers determine if the seat is installed correctly. Others use Bluetooth-enabled chest clips to send notifications to your phone if the chest clip breaks free mid-ride or if you walk away from your car while your child is still buckled in. A few models even have crash detection, which can send notifications to designated emergency contacts if a collision is detected.

The biggest difference comes down to how the technology is integrated. Some models, like the Cybex I tested, rely on a Bluetooth chest clip that connects to an app. Babyark takes a slightly different approach, with mechanical indicators on its Classic model and a swankier electronic sensor system built into the base of its higher-end Smart and Premium models.

The first thing I noticed about the Babyark out of the box was its base setup, which was different from any other car seats I’ve used. The base is a spaceship-looking device with a fold-out support leg and anti-rebound bar. The seat itself is pretty bulky, but I didn’t mind too much, since by the time I started using it, my daughter was old enough that I didn’t need to haul her around in an infant seat anymore.

Car seat installation can be an exercise in patience, but I found setup pretty straightforward. The Babyark app walked me through every step, with video tutorials for each stage. Once everything was in place, indicators on the base glowed green. (Red means something’s off.)

The app is easy to navigate, but once I installed the seat, I pretty much forgot about it. I enabled notifications in case something needed attention, but in my several months of using the seat, nothing has warranted an alert so far, aside from the occasional random disconnection.

It’s worth noting that the Babyark offers different versions of the seat, all with different technology. The Classic model, which I have, currently retails at $790 and offers guided installation videos and mechanical indicators. Babyark's Smart and Premium models—which retail for $999 and $1,190, respectively—add features like forgotten child alerts and impact detection. That’s a roughly $200 to $400 jump, which is worth considering if you’re particularly interested in those features.

You can check the app for basic statistics, like how much time your child spends in the seat, but I haven’t felt the need to follow this closely. More importantly, I didn’t find myself opening the app to monitor the seat while my daughter was in it. At the end of the day, the Babyark feels like a regular car seat to me. But a great, sturdy car seat at that!

I also tried out the Cloud G Pro, which comes with SensorSafe, a Bluetooth chest clip that communicates with the Cybex app on your phone. Pairing the clip, which looks and functions like any other, with my phone was easy peasy. When I intentionally tested the alerts, they worked as expected and came through almost immediately.

The temperature notifications worked, but almost too well. SensorSafe sends an alert when your car’s interior climbs to above 95 degrees Fahrenheit or drops below 45. Depending on the weather, your car might already be outside that range when you first get in, and it takes a little time for the cabin to warm up or cool down. So don’t be surprised if you get an alert before the AC or heat has a chance to do its thing.

SensorSafe can also alert you if the clip becomes unbuckled while driving or if you leave your child buckled in the seat and walk away with your phone. In the latter scenario, the default setting has your phone loudly announce “CHILD IN CAR!” in a man’s deep voice, which scared the hoots out of me the first time it went off. If you don’t respond to the alert (you can stop or snooze it), the app will notify your emergency contact and share your location.

Like the Babyark, I didn’t find myself opening the Cybex app very often to check on things. I mostly let it run in the background and waited for notifications rather than actively checking in on the system. The alerts worked just fine, but I used the app so infrequently that my phone eventually offloaded it.

As appealing as all those gadgets and gizmos sound, car seats aren’t foolproof. “These are supplements. They're not substitutes,” says Jennifer Booge, a car seat safety expert with the National Safety Council. “We have to make sure that we're understanding how to use the car seat correctly, because there is so much to know, and every car seat is so different.”

According to data collected through the NSC’s National Digital Car Seat Check Form, a little over 72 percent of car seats entered into the system have some form of misuse. Manufacturers are working to address these issues with installation videos and app-based guidance, but Booge says there’s still not enough research to determine whether smart features actually improve safety.

Some car seat manufacturers offer access to certified child passenger safety technicians who can walk you through installation questions. I experienced this firsthand with the Babyark. Even after following the app’s instructions and getting the green light that everything was secure, I still had some reservations about how much the seat was wiggling. I reached out to the company, and they virtually walked me through the installation. (Which turned out to be correct; car seats are supposed to have a slight wiggle, no more than an inch back and forth.)

“Don't be afraid to pick up the phone and call or schedule that virtual appointment and meet with those experts that are there to help you, because it's not easy,” Booge says. “Every car seat is different. Every vehicle and car seat combination is different.”

As Booge points out, tech can be useful even when it isn’t built into the seat itself. The rise of virtual appointments gives caregivers access to certified technicians that they may not otherwise have available. At the end of the day, a car seat doesn’t need a battery or an app to do its job, and all the technology in the world can’t replace knowing how to use it properly.

Do you need a smart car seat? Probably not. After testing the Babyark and the Cybex Cloud G Pro with SensorSafe, I’m not totally convinced the added tech is worth paying a premium for. Both offered features I appreciated, and they certainly gave me peace of mind, but neither fundamentally changed how I use a car seat day to day. I’d rather prioritize a seat that fits my child and my vehicle, and that I can use correctly, rather than pay extra for an app I rarely open. All in all, my biggest takeaway is not to mistake more features for more safety.

#363. Tesla’s Cybercab Is the Subscription Hell They Told You Not to Worry About

There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.

Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet's Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox, offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks, but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s "limited release” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December.

From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.

The business model raises questions about what people will actually get when they buy a Cybercab. “You’ll never really own the car,” says Ivan Drury, the director of insights at Edmunds. “It’s more like $30,000 to buy into a franchise.”

According to documents posted on Tesla’s website, the vehicle “will not operate” without what Tesla is calling an “autonomy subscription," a monthly fee that will start at $299. If owners don’t pay on time and in full, their self-driving cars won’t work. If they try to operate the vehicles in areas that don’t support the service—right now, they’re restricted to portions of cities in Florida and Texas—their self-driving cars won’t work. (That area can expand, contract, or “relocate” at any time.)

If owners do anything that Tesla deems "unauthorized or inappropriate," the company says it can suspend or cancel the subscription—and their self-driving cars won’t work. If the vehicle loses connectivity, the self-driving cars won’t work. (“Tesla is not responsible for carrier, spectrum, environmental, or other external outages,” its “autonomy agreement” says.)

Tesla also reserves the right to make an owner’s car not work at any time: It says it can, for any safety or security purpose, suspend or terminate access to Cybercab tech, or restrict operations by location, road type, weather, or “condition.” This is particularly salient because the Cybercab is also under investigation by US safety regulators, who are trying to understand why Tesla believes the vehicle meets safety standards without so many of the parts and systems required.

Tesla didn’t respond to a request for comment.

For years, automakers have seen increasingly software-dominated vehicles as an opportunity to get drivers hooked on the same special sauce that makes Netflix, Amazon, and Spotify so potent: monthly subscription services. Because these vehicles can receive over-the-air software updates, manufacturers can offer drivers new services as they make them. The upside is high, tech-style margins that keep rolling in, versus the razor-thin ones seen in car-making. A 2024 report suggested that connected-car features could one day be a $200 billion industry.

In some ways, the subscription model is working. Today, some automakers charge extra for remote start, security, internet connectivity, and advanced driver assistance features. General Motors said it made $2.7 billion in subscription-related revenue last year from fees drivers paid for its OnStar and Super Cruise services.

But some customers have also found the business model yucky, or even offensive. Why charge extra to “unlock” a feature that’s already built into a car? If an automaker can add a new feature at any time, can’t they also take it away? And if they can take it away, what does "ownership" mean? In 2022, BMW told drivers in select countries it would activate factory-installed heated seats for a monthly or one-time fee; it eventually backed down after public outcry, pledging the company would no longer charge subscription fees for pre-installed hardware. (BMW is still pursuing a subscription model for some features.) “Consumers hate being nickel-and-dimed for subscriptions,” says Drury.

Tesla was an early mover in the subscription feature space and has offered connectivity and driver-assistance features for monthly or one-time fees for a decade. As the company has shifted away from making cars and toward robotics and autonomous vehicles, executives have made clear that charging for services is the future. (Its Robotaxi service currently picks up fare-paying passengers in parts of eight US cities.) So Tesla buyers may be particularly amenable to paying monthly to make their self-driving cars go.

In exchange for monthly fees, buyers will also get access to other services, too, including remote support, roadside assistance, tire, air filter, and windshield wiper replacements, and tire and camera inspections. (The agreement says that list might change, too.) Cybercabs will be able to “travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center,” the company says. The fee doesn't cover insurance.

Cybercab buyers will have other restrictions. The vehicle is for personal use only. Even though CEO Elon Musk has repeatedly said owners will be able to put their vehicles on Tesla’s wider Robotaxi network to make money during downtime, and even has an online interest form for those who want to own and operate their own Cybercab fleets, the current ownership agreement prohibits that. Buyers are also prohibited from selling or transferring their vehicles without Tesla’s written consent. The company “advises against” children under 13 riding in the Cybercab, and prohibits children from riding without an adult present.

In a post on X, Musk showed no apparent compunction about the Cybercab business model, but did say the monthly price for autonomy “is too high.” He wrote that the price should be “more like ~$115/month.”
