#361. Trump’s Oil Grab in Venezuela Is Testing the Country’s National Identity

Long-held beliefs in Venezuela about sovereign control over oil are fraying as the U.S. lays claim to the country’s oil reserves.

Long-held beliefs in Venezuela about sovereign control over oil are fraying as the U.S. lays claim to the country’s oil reserves.

Sunrise over the Cardón Refinery in Punta Cardón, Venezuela. Oil has shaped Venezuela to an extent rare outside the Middle East, becoming a defining feature of the country’s social fabric.Credit...Adriana Loureiro Fernandez for The New York Times

Simon Romero is a former Caracas bureau chief who has covered energy politics across Latin America. Isayen Herrera reports on Venezuela for The New York Times.

Like generations before him, Leonardo Silva grew up steeped in beliefs about the extraordinarily abundant resource that made Venezuela special. All the oil under their feet was theirs, they felt. Virtually free gasoline was a birthright. To be born atop this bounty was like winning the lottery.

Mr. Silva, 38, said his generation viewed oil as a cornerstone of the country’s national identity, when a booming economy allowed Venezuela to occupy a privileged tier in the global order. His children, he said, have a far less rosy view.

“To them oil isn’t important, it’s secondary,” said Mr. Silva, who works at a foundation in Caracas helping people with disabilities. “They don’t have that culture of us being a rich country. They just know that if you don’t work, you don’t eat.”

Oil has shaped Venezuela to an extent that is rare outside the Middle East for more than a century, becoming a defining feature of the social fabric like baseball, beauty pageants or the veneration of the liberation hero Simón Bolívar.

But now the U.S. government is taking control of a huge portion of Venezuela’s oil. And, pressed by economic need, long-held nationalist convictions about oil, starting with the need for sovereign control, are giving way to a more complex web of perspectives.

The ways in which Venezuelans are re-evaluating oil, and by extension their reliance on it, are the result of immense upheaval over the last decade. Oil production plummeted because of mismanagement, political purges, corruption and sanctions.

#360. SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch

STARBASE, Texas—The black-and-silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontally until the last moment, when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.

Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about 1 foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.

Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.

This was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.

Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power and be captured by the tower.

It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks.

Humans have built reusable spacecraft that flew into orbit before. In the 1970s, flush with confidence after the triumphant Moon landings, NASA designed and built several Space Shuttles. They had solid rocket boosters that were fished from the ocean and reused. The large orange external tank was not recovered after each flight, but the orbiters went to space for two weeks, or even longer, before returning to Earth and landing on a runway.

The shuttles were engineering marvels. But during the return to Earth they acted as gliders, not igniting their engines. And their heat shields were delicate flowers, requiring painstaking refurbishment after each flight. At the outset of the shuttle program, the space agency contemplated sending dozens of humans into space at a time, and carrying cargo at a cost as low of $25 per pound.

Reality never matched these rosy projections. The crew space capped out at seven astronauts, and the cost-per-pound was closer to $25,000. Each orbiter cost an extraordinary amount of money to build; NASA only ever built five that went to space.

SpaceX has five Starships in an advanced state of development at Starbase today; and its factory houses the components for a dozen more. The company can currently manufacture a Starship upper stage in its South Texas Starfactory every three weeks. The factory was sized to produce a ship every three days. When SpaceX founder Elon Musk discussed these build targets in an interview five years ago, he sounded mad. But he no longer does.

The Space Shuttle was nearly a fully reusable space launch system, but it fell far short of low-cost rapid launch. Over 30 years the vehicle made 135 flights. Within a few years SpaceX aims to fly 135 times a year, then thousands of times.

Such was the significance of Saturday. SpaceX aspires to fundamentally change the relationship between humanity and the heavens. The first step is to get the entire rocket back. SpaceX has now returned both elements of a Starship rocket safely to its launch tower. It will take time to reach a high rate of success with such landings, but Saturday’s safe return offered a proof of concept.

The landings will come with increasing frequency; and so will the launches. Over time SpaceX will perfect the heat shield that is likely to be the most difficult aspect of rapid reuse. And eventually, as difficult as it may be to believe, what we experienced with amazement this weekend will become routine. One day, we will take this all for granted.

#358. AI Told These Ex-Google Guys How to Build a Billion-Dollar Weapons Business

When Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start. So the then CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today, he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defense-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion.

Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style. They believe their experience building and iterating technology quickly can help bring Western weapon manufacturing in line with the rapid innovation cycles seen on the battlefield and beat the “attritional cat-and-mouse technology game” that the war, as Baynes describes it, has become.

Steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022. He says he was regularly “heartbroken” by the outpouring of grief whenever bad news arrived about a husband, father, or son back home. “I believe I could really change the outcome of this and every war,” Steelberg tells WIRED. "I'm not saying this is purely altruistic,” he adds. “Of course we're going to be making money doing it."

This week, their firm, Tiberius Aerospace, said it had secured $85 million in Series A financing, led by European technology investment firm Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management, a national-security-focused investment firm licensed under the US Defense Department. Ukrainian venture capital firm UA1 is also an investor.

Tiberius began as Steelberg’s private research lab, incorporated in 2021, which employed people across France, the UK, and US to experiment on left-field ideas across a range of technologies, from drones and electric vertical takeoff aircraft to quantum computing. After the invasion, he pivoted the lab’s AI and aerospace engineers into writing code and building spreadsheets to objectively analyze the war’s many factors and calculate what could move the needle. The AI model they created quickly ruled out building better defensive technology because that would just harden the stalemate.

With his aim narrowed to building an offensive weapon, Steelberg developed several metrics to numerically analyze the lethality of different systems, including cost-effectiveness, and used the AI engine to simulate weapons under different conditions and identify what would disrupt the market. Don’t build another drone, it suggested, build longer-range artillery munitions. The resulting system, called Sceptre, can be fired from a 155-millimeter howitzer—the most common artillery weapon donated to Ukraine. As well as traveling farther than currently available rounds, they claim they can reach supersonic speeds and altitudes beyond jamming range.

Giving Ukraine’s guns extra range is important, Sam Cranny-Evans, an associate fellow at UK defense think tank the Royal United Services Institute, tells WIRED, because it would allow Ukrainian gunners to operate beyond the reach of Russian drone attacks. 155-mm shells “can cause massive damage to a group of vehicles or infantry,” he says. “Any technology that can help Ukraine extend the reach of its howitzers and return them to combat would be valuable.”

With a prototype he’d designed with the help of AI, Steelberg also started to expand the Tiberius team, including bringing on board Baynes as chief strategy officer in 2023. Baynes had first traveled to Ukraine around a decade ago to investigate how local startup Ring, now owned by Amazon, had outdone Nest, which he’d been working on and eventually sold to Google. He fell in love with Kyiv’s ambitious software engineers and booming tech scene–responsible for globally successful tech tools like Grammarly and Snapchat’s face filters. In 2016, he bought a local life-science tech company with the aim of accelerating next-generation medicines through automating clinical trials and improving protein modeling. “What drew me into Kyiv was the hunger and ambition in the engineering community,” he tells WIRED. “It was difficult to not be enormously attracted to that and to see if it's something that could be put into really critical-mission problem sets like cancer drugs or speeding up clinical trials for life-science companies.”

After the Russian invasion, Baynes set himself up in Budapest for around six months to help with the logistics of evacuating women and children and moving equipment into the country. He asked his global network for help finding medical equipment, vehicles, and accommodation for refugees—bringing him back in touch with Steelberg. Baynes believes the West’s response to the invasion has been “inadequate” and that Ukraine needs better offensive capabilities to push Russia’s army back.

In April, Tiberius announced it had successfully fired one of its Sceptre projectiles from a NATO-standard 155-mm howitzer for the first time. It is now working with the US Army to mature the system, and it has announced a $500 million technology collaboration contract with UK partners to manufacture, license, and distribute the munition. It is also developing a missile, which it expects to start generating revenue next year.

Tiberius has turned the AI system it initially built into a product called GRAIL (Generative Real-Time Artificial Intelligence for Lethality). Steelberg says he is “most excited about” this. He hopes the platform can enable continuous upgrades to the weapon designs Tiberius licenses by decentralizing manufacturing. Steelberg says that, as well as automating supply chain management and compliance, the software simulates weapons against different targets in a range of environments and weather conditions, such as an Arctic peninsula. In addition to open-sourced data, the team is trying to get hold of much sought-after active combat data from around the world, including Ukraine. The idea is that this all enables users to test, iterate, and design weapons for specific uses much quicker.

“In the world of AI and design and development getting faster and faster, what is it that the West or the group of allied nations have an undeniable advantage on?” Baynes asks. “If you can weaponize all of the spare capacity and precision manufacturing across the UK, France, Germany, the Nordic countries, the US,” he says, “that's something that our adversaries today can never ever match.” Tiberius aims to achieve this by copying “the Apple model,” continues Baynes, who reported to Steve Jobs for four years. He says outsourcing manufacturing to many third-party subcontractors can accelerate development and deployment and keeps expensive production costs off Tiberius’ balance sheet during peacetime.

“We're taking the approach of Silicon Valley,” says Steelberg. “When you run into a big, hard, hairy problem, you not only cross that, but you turn around, you build a bridge—it’s a toll bridge, obviously—so the entire industry can cross that hurdle faster, better, stronger. They might pay a small fee, but it's better than dying in the ditch and not making it across it.”

#356. In Canada, Watching the N.H.L. Has Become Expensive and Cumbersome

Games behind paywalls and exorbitant costs forcing a drop in attendance — even to watch Connor McDavid in Edmonton — have only compounded the loss of a Saturday night ritual.

The National Hockey League season is less than two months old, and much of the focus in Canada has been on how expensive it is to attend games, and how costly and cumbersome it has become to watch them on television.

Attendance has fallen in several markets, including Edmonton, where Connor McDavid has an astonishing 49 points in 20 games and is on pace to challenge Wayne Gretzky’s single-season scoring record of 215 points.

This week, The Globe and Mail reported that three TV providers had filed a complaint with the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission asking Rogers Sportsnet to reverse its decision to put more than 50 Monday night N.H.L. games behind a paywall on its streaming service for an extra $13 a month.

Further increasing the cost and complexity of watching hockey, Wednesday night games are on Prime Video. TSN broadcasts some regional games with blackouts, and a subscription to NHL Centre Ice is needed to watch out-of-market games.

Until this season, the N.H.L. could be found for free.

In June, the CBC and Rogers Sportsnet announced that the national broadcaster would no longer air N.H.L. games on Saturday nights, a first in 75 years, ending the cultural institution “Hockey Night in Canada.” Last month, the CBC announced it would begin airing Professional Women’s Hockey League games when its season begins in December.

#355. How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause

COVID-19 lockdowns cut global fire activity by 12.3 percent.

Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.

Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.

A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.

Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without big fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.

Weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.

Human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.

The double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.

Sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.

An experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.

Wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”

The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.

In the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.

The results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.

Controlling for weather factors was important in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.

The 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.

Wang said, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”

In regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.

There are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.

One line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires showed a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.

Mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.

When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.

This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.

Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.

Wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be important. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.

Wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

Cell Reports Sustainability, 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.crsus.2026.100860

#354. How a Bunch of YouTube Auteurs Are Reinventing Hollywood

The mad scramble to score Imax tickets for The Odyssey was about as intense as the Trojan War, and the Marvel Cinematic Universe showed signs of resurgence with Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s $2.5 billion global haul. But the biggest buzz of the 2026 summer movie season? Two small-scale horror films from a couple of young YouTube auteurs.

First came Obsession, from 27-year-old Curry Barker, which made more than $500 million worldwide on a budget of less than $1 million. The film follows a meek young man named Bear, who yearns to be in a romantic relationship with his friend Nikki and uses a magical object to make his wish come true. By turns moody, funny, and shocking, Obsession proved that audiences are hungry to talk about something other than reheated IP. Barker got his start with the YouTube sketch comedy channel That’s a Bad Idea, while 21-year-old Kane Parsons gained a cult following on the platform by experimenting with visual effects and creepy atmospherics. A series of short films Parsons made in his teens culminated with the release of Backrooms in May. The feature picked up the narrative from those earlier YouTube videos, which were themselves inspired by an old 4chan meme and internet folklore around the idea of haunted liminal spaces.

Parsons’ avid fandom anticipated a big-screen Backrooms long before he signed with A24, making the movie a guaranteed hit. Backrooms earned $400 million worldwide on a budget of $10 million, surpassing Marty Supreme as the studio’s highest-grossing movie ever. The film stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Clark, a depressed divorcé who runs a failing furniture warehouse and vents about his ruined marriage to his therapist. One night, when investigating his store’s glitchy electrical system, he stumbles through a wall and into an apparently infinite maze of fluorescent-lit hallways that contain what seem to be deconstructed or misremembered pieces of the real world—and perhaps some living entities as well.

Though Backrooms stands alone as a hallucinatory vision of a vast, ever-expanding unreality just outside our own, many critics also read it as commentary on the state of generative artificial intelligence, which mindlessly reproduces and regurgitates its training data in permutations that often don’t make sense. Whether Parsons intended that interpretation or not, he spoke out against AI several times following the movie’s release, calling it “a symptom of a broader cultural and economic rot.”

The people, inventions, and viral moments that made 2026 a little more bearable.

Something we missed? Let us know in the comments.

Then there’s Zach Cregger. While not a YouTuber per se, he got his start in sketch comedy (The Whitest Kids U’ Know) and this year followed 2025’s Weapons with a 2026 adaptation of Resident Evil.

Parsons told WIRED earlier in the year that he imagines his cohort of directors will bring certain YouTube sensibilities to Hollywood. “I don’t think there’s a lot of Instagram filmmakers or a lot of TikTok filmmakers that go for long-form content in a way that would actually be looked at or respected as film,” he says. “So it feels like YouTube is the only viable avenue in that way, in an actual meaningful mainstream context.” Among the crop of twentysomething filmmakers entering the industry today, “I think it’s very unlikely that you would have a filmmaker who is sort of reaching that place right now and getting that kind of media attention who has not at some point in the last 20 years put stuff on YouTube,” Parsons says.

Studios have certainly taken notice, scouting the site’s horror content for fresh talent and aggressively pursuing breakout projects. After a screening of Barker’s Obsession at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025, A24 and Neon embarked on a bidding war for the film before it was picked up by Focus Features for roughly $15 million.

Netflix reportedly also lost out on a bid to take Obsession straight to streaming; it’s possible that other young directors will follow Barker’s example in pushing for theatrical release.

The YouTube generation is proving that the internet can supply whatever education you might need on your path to the red carpet. While Hollywood consolidation threatens to stifle creativity, a new wave of artists are betting on themselves—and some are winning.

#350. Rogue Agents Hacked His Company. Why Is Clément Delangue So Optimistic About AI?

Clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face, may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree.

As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The company’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai.

Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, says the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone.

Despite championing the democratization of AI, however, Hugging Face was acquired by one of the industry’s biggest players, Nvidia, for $12.93 billion in September. When I caught up with Delangue recently, that was the subject of my first question.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

CLÉMENT DELANGUE: We need more resources to give open-source AI a chance. It has grown really well in the past few years and has become a really credible alternative to closed-source APIs. But the field is still dominated by closed-source.

We’re gonna have the Anthropic IPO in a few weeks. They basically went from zero to a top five or top 10 most valuable company in the world in a few years. I don't think that's ever happened before.

The people, inventions, and viral moments that made 2026 a little more bearable.

Something we missed? Let us know in the comments.

Does Anthropic's IPO suggest the closed approach is winning?

It’s hard to say. I've always said that there is a very strong natural tendency for AI to concentrate capabilities and wealth. People haven't internalized how much of the future compute capacity has already been reserved by a few companies. Talent, compute, resources—these all fuel the natural tendency for AI to be dominated by a few closed-source labs.

Let’s talk about the attack. When did you first realize Hugging Face was being hacked by a group of AI agents?

At the beginning, it didn't go to the top of our priority list. It just wasn't bad enough to really trigger that. The goal was pretty narrow and wasn’t deemed to be very dangerous or damaging. But it was raising questions. Especially the number of actions taken compared to the narrowness of the goal. It was surprising to us, and we couldn't really fit it into a familiar pattern. That's why we started investigating.

And you used the Chinese model called GLM to investigate.

I actually think that 95 percent of the risks are being created by a few companies that are pushing the frontier behind closed doors. And 95 percent of the protection or defense is going to be done by the open-source ecosystem.

Does the US need its own open-weight models—ones as powerful as GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen?

Yeah, I think it's very, very important for sovereignty, for understanding AI, and for academia. It’s kind of weird that most academic labs have to use Chinese models because they’re the ones that are open. If you go to Stanford or MIT, you have no choice but to use the Chinese open-weight models.

There is some momentum, but I don't think it's enough. I think there's a lot more to do. A lot more investment is needed.

The best open-source non-Chinese models are actually coming from outside of the US. Right from France, Mistral; Cohere from Canada; South Korea is starting to do more and more. But it’s still pretty far from what the US could do.

Perhaps we don’t need to panic about AI agents, but what about the idea of AI escaping human control due to recursive self-improvement?

You use a computer to write code. There's already some form of self-improvement in using the tools to build more tools. Now the question is how fast it accelerates. One thing that a lot of people realized this summer is that keeping AI behind closed doors in a few labs isn't actually safer. For recursive self-improvement, I think openness is a way to understand, follow, and regulate if we need to regulate.

Can we talk about the Microduck? I’m a bit obsessed.

Oh yeah, it's so fun, no? We're probably gonna sell over 50,000 of them this year. It's probably the most popular robot of the year.

We haven't talked about this much, but AI was really the unlock for the robot. We had the design for two years, but the problem was that when it fell, it couldn’t get up. And then at some point with reinforcement learning, one of our software engineers managed to get the Microduck to get itself back up.

At the end of the day, how do you convince people to take an interest in open-source AI?

Think of a world where two or three companies could write software and nobody else. That would be incredibly scary. It would mean that the whole world would be controlled by two or three companies. And unfortunately, that's kind of the direction that AI is taking right now.

Can open-source AI compete with something as capable as Claude or ChatGPT?

Yes, especially with agents. Many companies have shown that when you post-train your own model for your own use case, you get frontier—or even better than frontier—performance at a fraction of the cost.

Do you think we are getting close to AGI?

I struggle a little bit with the meaning of that. Obviously the technology is progressing incredibly fast, and it’s more and more capable. I just don’t necessarily find it super useful to always compare AI to human capabilities. But if we’re getting to AGI or to superintelligence, it’s incredibly important that it’s as distributed as possible. The last thing you want is to have it concentrated in a few corporations.

#348. Ukraine’s Starshield Access Is Being Restricted Again, Zelensky Says

President Volodymyr Zelensky said the system, which Ukraine uses to guide drones, was being throttled over Russian-occupied territory. SpaceX, its developer, has denied the claim.

Ukrainian military operations were disrupted again this week along the front lines because of restrictions on Starshield, the satellite internet system developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and controlled by the U.S. government, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday.

Mr. Zelensky told reporters that speed limits of about 100 miles per hour were being enforced for Ukrainian devices connected to the system. It would be the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine’s Starshield connectivity had been throttled. The previous restrictions caused Ukrainian drones to lose their connection to the system if they flew above certain speeds.

Mr. Zelensky said that the latest speed limits took effect on Monday and were being enforced over Russian-occupied territories, not over all of Ukraine. That hurts Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian troops with drones in those territories.

Imposing restrictions on occupied territories is “very dangerous, because it already has political implications,” Mr. Zelensky said. “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” he added.

Mr. Zelensky said separately in his nightly speech that the Starshield limits hurt Ukraine’s ability to use newly developed interceptors to protect its cities from Russia’s jet-powered drones. It is likely, however, that those limits would not affect interceptors in Kyiv, the capital, which is being battered by jet-powered drones but is far from the front lines.

Mr. Musk and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment on Friday evening. SpaceX had earlier told Axios that the Ukrainian claim about throttled connectivity was false.

#346. Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors

This was the first total mission failure in United Launch Alliance’s 20-year history.

United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.

The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.

Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents triggered monthslong reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.

Sunday’s launch succumbed to a different kind of failure. The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after Vulcan’s liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC).

In a statement, ULA said the rocket “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The company said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred.”

“ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the company said in a statement. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.”

Engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible,” ULA said.

“ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.”

The first indications of trouble Sunday appeared to crop up before the 10-minute mark of the flight, the point in time when ULA initially said the anomaly occurred.

Multiple sources told Ars the anomaly that impacted the launch occurred in the booster stage of the rocket, not the Centaur V upper stage or the solid rocket boosters. It could not immediately be determined whether the booster stage issue was caused by the two methane-burning BE-4 engines that power it, some other part of the booster that feeds propellant into the engines, or another problem.

Heading northeast from Cape Canaveral, Vulcan jettisoned its spent solid rocket boosters on time, leaving the launcher flying on the power of its twin BE-4 main engines supplied by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’ space company. The BE-4s, each designed to produce more than a half-million pounds of thrust, were supposed to shut down just shy of the flight’s five-minute mark. However, they continued firing for at least 30 additional seconds.

Such an overburn could be an indication the booster stage was not performing as expected and operated longer to try to compensate for the underperformance.

A mission animation on ULA’s broadcast, driven by real-time telemetry data from the rocket, showed Vulcan start to spin moments after booster engine shutdown. The spin continued through separation of the rocket’s Centaur V upper stage a few seconds later. ULA’s launch commentator confirmed ignition of the Centaur’s two RL10 engines, and the animation showed them vectoring thrust in an apparent attempt to put the rocket back on course.

ULA ended its live broadcast a few minutes later without discussion of the anomaly. The company then released a statement on social media declaring the launch a failure. This was the first total mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its formation in 2006 with the merger of the rocket divisions of Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

Sunday’s incident is bad news for ULA’s two primary customers: Amazon and the US Space Force. It’s also a potential setback for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon.

First, Amazon. The loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard the Vulcan rocket is, by itself, a secondary concern next to the inevitable grounding of the company’s primary launch provider. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.

The Amazon Leo constellation today consists of 396 satellites, a fraction of the network’s planned total of 3,292 first-generation spacecraft. Amazon officials told Ars in October that the company has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more launches are required to realize the network’s full capacity.

Amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers, not directly to consumers.

Previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the company planned. Amazon recently announced it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket.

“There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon said in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

Amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’ Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan launches in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that company’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have launched so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.

Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but luckily for Amazon, the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time.

What’s more, the New Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year.

That would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, Bezos’ chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement.

It’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s New Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads.

Vulcan’s earlier delays forced Space Force officials to move six national security launches from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials used the swaps to get time-sensitive payloads into space sooner on Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, rather than waiting for Vulcan. In exchange, the Space Force awarded a future SpaceX mission to ULA.

Expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday. For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit.

But SpaceX has made it clear Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy won’t be around much longer. Musk’s company is rapidly transitioning to Starship to launch its own Starlink satellites and new orbiting AI-powered compute platforms. SpaceX has not revealed plans yet to certify Starship for national security missions, a process that would take multiple years.

Amazon will likely have to use the 10 Falcon 9 launches it has already reserved and Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket to add any more Amazon Leo satellites to the network in the coming months. Blue Origin’s New Glenn, once it returns to flight, has a series of backlogged launches for NASA’s Artemis Moon program next year, including key test flights of Blue’s lunar lander to prepare for future human missions. Those Moon lander tests could be pushed back further if the BE-4 engine was at fault for Sunday’s failure.

NASA’s lunar program has another important link to the Vulcan rocket. The space agency recently announced it selected a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, the vehicle used for launching astronaut crews to the Moon. The Centaur will replace a more expensive, unproven Boeing upper stage design. NASA officials will want to rule out a problem with the Centaur V upper stage on Sunday’s doomed launch as the agency aims to start flying ULA’s Centaur on SLS missions for crewed lunar flights as soon as 2028.

“Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote in reply to ULA’s statement on the Vulcan launch anomaly. “The team at NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.”

#344. The Apple Watch’s Live Rewind Can Record and Rewind Spoken Conversations. It’s Pretty Awkward

My wife and I were driving back from a date night. She was talking about a friend's very expensive utility bill, but I had missed the beginning of what she said (I was driving, after all).

Then I remembered: Wait, I can ask Siri to remind me! At a traffic light, I double-tapped the digital crown on the Apple Watch, and Siri's new Live Rewind feature spun back the clock 15 seconds and showed me a transcript of what my wife said.

I sheepishly interrupted her to show her the transcript. “Look!” Her reply? “Why wouldn't you just ask me to repeat myself?” She shrugged at this new Apple Watch capability and continued talking.

A few days later, I was chatting with my brother on my stoop. Once again, I lost focus for a few seconds and remembered to ask Siri to help me recall what my brother said moments ago. But this time, before I excitedly showed my brother the Apple Watch screen, I preemptively said, “Yeah, I know I could just ask you to repeat yourself.” I got a perplexed look back.

Live Rewind, one of Apple's new Audio Intelligence features on its latest Apple Watches, is designed to give you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. It's in public beta in watchOS 27.3, but is expected to launch officially before the year's end.

Coming alongside it is another new capability called Siri Recap: Give the assistant permission to listen to your environment—you can set schedules or have it trigger when you reach the office—and you'll see a “Recap” in the Siri app at the end of the day. It’ll show you summaries of conversations and list out important details that people said. It's very similar to AI notetakers, many of which run on dedicated hardware devices.

“One of the concerns that we have with things like the Apple Watch is we don't know what the watch is picking up on,” Reem Suleiman, senior campaign director at the nonprofit digital rights advocacy group Fight for the Future, tells WIRED. “Just because the device wearer is the one opting in to use the feature, you're not getting consent from everybody who you walk around.”

For Live Rewind, the audio is processed on-device and cannot be accessed. When you activate it, a small chime plays from the Apple Watch that serves as a warning for folks nearby. Text disappears unless you choose to save it to Siri. For Recaps, Siri keeps them factual, doesn't identify speakers, and also omits content the system deems sensitive. If you don't save a Recap, it'll self-delete in seven days. Apple uses its Private Cloud Compute processing system for the data, which is never stored or logged on its servers. Data stored in the Siri app is end-to-end encrypted when syncing with iCloud.

Siri Recaps are stored in the Siri app and will self-delete in seven days if you do not save them.

Activating it in front of the person you're chatting with feels awkward. It comes across like pulling out your smartphone when someone's trying to talk to you—a little rude and distracting. Instead of keeping screens out of sight—a big digital detox trend—you're introducing one in the middle of a human conversation. I brought the topic up with my wife again, and she echoed some of those feelings, saying it felt like a feature that would stunt a person's social skills. Instead of asking someone to repeat themself, they're bringing an Apple Watch into the mix to fill in the gaps.

I am not saying it can't be helpful. When it works, it feels like a superpower. Maybe there are certain situations where you don't want to interrupt a group conversation and ask someone to repeat themself. Right now, though, there's the problem of remembering that this feature exists and remembering to use it. I have also found the 15-second rule a little too short, and it resulted in me missing parts of the conversation.

Recap has been a little more helpful. For testing purposes, I've set Siri to capture recaps all day, every day, but I like that you can create a custom schedule or have it trigger when you arrive at a specific location, like the office. You can manually turn Siri Recap on or off in the Apple Watch's Control Center. Most impressive is that, despite having Recap enabled constantly, I haven't seen a meaningful dip in battery life. I've continued charging the Apple Watch Series 12 after a day and a half.

Siri Recap logs summaries of ambient conversations.

One of the more perplexing things was opening the Siri app to look at my recaps and finding a bunch of conversations I had no recollection of having. Turns out, Siri was recording media I was watching, like on YouTube or Instagram. This is a problem I encountered with AI notetakers, like the Amazon-owned Bee AI wearable, which claimed to be working on “liveness detection” to solve it. Its latest hardware shipped with a feature where it doesn't record a conversation if it doesn't detect the wearer's voice within a set period. Hopefully, Apple can figure out a solution. For now, you can edit or delete these recaps.

One day, I forgot to record an interview (though I took notes), and I knew the person said something that I hadn't written down. I headed over to Siri and found exactly what I was looking for—paraphrased, but there. That said, the Recaps aren't designed to be detailed summaries and action plans from your meetings or conversations, unlike dedicated AI notetakers. They're meant to jog your memory. At times, I wish Siri were more detailed, but if that's what you're after, you'll have to invest in a third-party device.

Recap can be helpful for work meetings, but I haven't personally found it all that compelling in my personal life. Looking back at what it has picked up over conversations with friends and family, the only thing I feel is: Yep, those conversations happened. A friend was talking about their woodworking hobby—they can't use oil-based polyurethane as a finish in the winter months as it stays tacky. Siri logged this in such a matter-of-fact way, but when I revisited the conversation in the recap, I didn't find it helpful, useful, or interesting. (No offense, friend!) It's just nuggets of life.

#341. Here’s the latest.

Carmelle of the Philippines defeated 10 competitors at the first edition of the high-camp event in Asia, held in Bangkok.

The Eurovision Song Contest crowned its first Asia champion in Bangkok on Saturday, in an event that tested whether a high-camp singing competition with an ardent fan base could appeal to audiences in a new market.

Carmelle of the Philippines was declared the winner of the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, beating out artists and original songs from 10 other countries: Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. The show was live-streamed on YouTube and broadcast by television stations across the region.

Eurovision has been a fixture of the European cultural calendar since it began in 1956. Past winners include Sweden’s ABBA and the Canadian chanteuse Celine Dion, who represented Switzerland in 1988.

Asian artists have readily embraced the kitschy outfits and spectacular sets that are part of Eurovision tradition, with costumes that include traditional dress, as well as feathered capes and sequined corsets. Malaysia’s performer plans to enter the stage in a giant teardrop.

But the Eurovision format has not been tested in Asia. Fans and regional partners have expressed concern in recent weeks that budget constraints, production issues and weak audience demand could imperil the spinoff. Organizers say the contest could take time to build an audience.

“It would be profoundly arrogant to think that just because we have a heritage brand and a huge global audience for the European show, that we would walk in and demand it to be the same here,” said Martin Green, the European Broadcasting Union’s director of the Eurovision Song Contest. “Like any new thing, it needs to find its roots.”

Two previous attempts to take the competition to Asia were abandoned by the European Broadcasting Union, which owns Eurovision, and its partners in the region. A Eurovision spinoff in the United States, NBC’s American Song Contest, ran for one season in 2022.

The Asian edition kicking off on Saturday is far smaller than its European counterpart. Eurovision organizers said they were in talks with more countries to join future seasons. They include China, Japan and India, whose music industries have global reach.

“Bringing the world together through music is a fundamentally good idea,” Mr. Green said. “Europe shouldn’t keep it to itself.”

Ballads: Nine of the competition’s 11 participating countries picked performers singing about love in a wide range of styles, from ballads to a cappella hip-hop. Their choices suggest that the bombastic music often associated with victors of the European edition might not be a winning formula for Asian viewers. Read more ›

Fans: Our reporter spoke to some of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for Eurovision. Read more ›

Politics: Geopolitics have long intruded on the European edition of the Eurovision Song Contest, but they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia. Read more ›

No shows: For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia has several notable absences, starting with China and India. Read more ›

As Thailand’s Mang and Daou waited to learn whether they had won, the 26-year-old Mang was shown onscreen crying as if she couldn’t take the tension. That’s the sort of emotion needed to make Eurovision’s expansion into Asia a success. Acts have to want the title. But the show will also need the big Asian nations -- India, Japan and China -- to buy in, and much could now depend on the reaction in the Philippines to Carmelle’s win. The event was far less spectacular than a typical Eurovision in Europe. It also featured far too many ballads for my taste, but it was a fun afternoon’s viewing.

Shiesam Flores, 27, a clerk from the eastern region of Bicol in the Philippines, has been watching the show at a party with her friends — and hoping that Carmelle would prevail.

“It was nerve-wracking, nail biting suspense!” she said. “But we know she would win! What a talent!”

The Philippines’ Carmelle wins the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, pushing Thailand’s Mang and Daou into second.

The crowd roared in disappointment as Malaysia got only 70 points from the public vote.

Thailand takes a massive lead thanks to the public vote, but the genius of this voting process is we won’t know whether the Philippines can overcome them until the last seconds.

The public gave Beatmosphere, from Bangladesh, just 19 points. They looked surprisingly happy after getting such a low total, and it’s now confirmed they’ve come in a distant last.

Dara has brought the Eurovision Asia trophy to the stage. It’s a sparkly gold microphone.

The public vote can be brutal, as some acts rapidly learn that few viewers liked them.

The jury votes are all in, and it’s close. The Philippines is first with 93 points, Vietnam second with 83 points and Malaysia third with 82 points. We’re about to learn how many points each country’s act received from the public, starting with the current last place act, Bangladesh’s beatboxing-heavy crew Beatmosphere. It has 16 points.

One of the best parts of Eurovision is how the public’s choice is often completely diffferent from those of the juries, so don’t worry if your favorite act isn’t top of the ranking after the jury votes are all in. The Philippine’s jury, the first we’ve heard from, just gave its 12 points to Malaysia. That doesn’t mean it’ll win

Fans are decked out in flags and sequins for the first-ever Asia Eurovision here in Bangkok.

The problem Eurovision has with interval acts like Jeff Satur is that their stagecraft, singing ability and melodies are often a million times better than the artists in competition. Satur, who has 1.4 million monthly listeners on Spotify and over five million Instagram fans, has dozens of camp dancers onstage and a statue of a dragon. He would have cruised to victory if he’d been in competition, especially because of his ability to hold high notes close to the range only dogs can hear.

Simon Robinson, one of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday, said that his history with the competition is nearly as long as its seven-decade run.

He was eight years old when he first watched it with his family in Yorkshire, England, when Britain's Mary Hopkin finished in second place behind Ireland’s Dana.

“I really liked the concept of bringing Europe together after the war,” said Mr. Robinson, 63, who now lives in Melbourne, Australia. He described the contest’s annual broadcast as a social activity for his family and neighbors.

“Eurovision helped to create the European identity,” he added.

Other fans had their own motivations for traveling to see the contest’s first Asian edition.

Some are Europeans living in Asia, on the hunt for nostalgia, while others are Americans who were eager to experience their first Eurovision.

Lee Hudson, an American television executive based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, said that he gets emotional when he talks about Eurovision, which he has watched since 2012.

“The only reason I know any music from European countries is because I heard them on Eurovision,” he said. “Eurovision Asia makes sense because the musical cultures are distinct.”

Mr. Hudson said he still listens to Loreen’s “Euphoria,” which won the competition for Sweden in 2012.

It was also the first Eurovision that Drew Andrea watched from his home in Sydney. A year later, he got a passport to fly to Sweden for the 2013 edition, and has attended every final since. Coming to Bangkok for Eurovision Asia was much more affordable, he said.

“Asia understands the brief — the kitschy costumes, the dance music,” he said.

His top picks among the Asian performers were the Philippines’ Carmelle and Vietnam’s Toc Tien. “I think they hit the nail on the head with the song, staging, costume and traditional elements,” he said.

Luca Cian, a professor of marketing at the University of Virginia who grew up in Italy, said that Eurovision built a global fan base by offering a shared cultural experience.

“Millions of people across Europe watch it at the same moment,” he said. “Families have watch parties with food and drinks. There are public discussions. Rituals create community.”

Carmen Chung, a British accountant, said she hijacked her family’s holiday in Bangkok to attend Eurovision Asia with her brother Garry Chung, a banker who lives in Hong Kong. “We were raised on Eurovision,” she said of their childhood in Yorkshire.

European acts, she said, tend to copy whatever style of music won the previous year. “This year, because there are no expectations, everyone has just done their own thing,” she said. She and her brother said they were rooting for Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere, a beatboxing group that will perform an a cappella love song.

Martin Green, the director of the Eurovision Song Contest, said that about half of the tickets for Saturday’s final were purchased by “super fans” from outside Asia. Organizers have kept the inaugural show modest, with 11 participating countries and a 5,000-seat venue.

Mr. Andrea said he didn’t mind the small scale.

“I’m O.K. with humble beginnings as long as it keeps growing every year,” he said.

The Thai pop star Jeff Satur, a guest performer, got the high-camp memo.

The presenters are talking to the artists in the green room and trying to get them to talk excitedly about Bulgaria, the country that will host the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest. The winner tonight might get to perform at that event. That seems to be making this show less about Asia itself than a spin-off of the main Eurovision event

Eurovision voting involves two parts. Juries representing music industry professionals from each country are allocated half the votes, and the viewing public decides the other half. To try to build tension, the show always announces the jury votes first by going live to representatives from each country who reveals their top acts. In the European edition of the contest, some of those spokespeople are celebrities, and often they try to give mini speeches or make jokes. This part of the show is always awful. You have been warned.

There are a lot of European expatriates in this crowd. That much is obvious when Bulgaria’s Dara, the winner of this year’s Eurovision, takes the stage with her winning song, “Bangaranga.” Some fans even danced along with her choreography!

Mohamad Iqbal Dzulqarnain, an Aina Abdul fan in Kuala Lumpur, said he felt her performance was better than the recording version.

“She left no crumbs,” he said. “She is going to win the contest.”

For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia on Saturday had several notable absences.

For starters, the continent’s four most populous nations — China, India, Pakistan and Indonesia — were not there. Even Japan, a country globally considered a cultural powerhouse, was absent.

That left some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix. India has Bollywood hits. China has produced both Mandopop and Cantopop, the genre associated with Hong Kong pop stars. JPop was once huge across Asia.

As a result, the only large pop powerhouse in this contest was South Korea.

China’s absence is relatively simple to explain. Performers are entered by local broadcasters, and Eurovision has long had a messy relationship with China’s, which are heavily regulated and try to reflect the government’s social and political values. Mango TV once had a deal to broadcast the high-camp Eurovision to Chinese viewers, but Eurovision abruptly canceled it in 2018 after Mango TV censored acts whose performances featured gay themes. It also blurred rainbow flags in the performance arena.

Frank-Dieter Freiling, a former Eurovision official, said in an interview that such censorship was against Eurovision’s values and that the show’s organizers had historically barred broadcasters from airing the competition with delays.

It’s less clear why broadcasters from India, Pakistan, Japan and Indonesia did not participate. Assaf Blecher, Eurovision Asia’s executive producer, said that conversations with Chinese, Japanese and Indian broadcasters had not concluded in time. But he insisted that they “are knocking on our door.”

Not participating saved those countries the potential embarrassment of being the regional power that comes in last.

Just look to Europe, where Britain and Germany often perform badly at Eurovision. In this year’s show, Britain’s Look Mum No Computer placed last, scoring only one point, while Germany finished third from last. Whenever that happens, political commentators give interviews suggesting that the results reflect those countries’ poor standing across Europe.

Here at the watch party in Kathmandu, Pratik’s relatives are happy with his performance.

“His voice was cracking during the selection round in Nepal,” said Sunita Rai, his sister-in-law. “Today’s performance was much more powerful.”

His relatives have been on social media all night, urging their friends who live overseas to vote for him. (You can’t vote for your own country’s performer.)

The presenters have just announced a technical issue! When Laos’s Thinla performed earlier, she had an earpiece problem and was unable to hear her own music. So that explains why she sang so out of tune. They’re now playing a recording of an earlier performance to everyone to try to ensure the event is fair

Rizal Kamal, a senior adviser to the Arts, Live Festival and Events Association, an entertainment nonprofit based in Malaysia, said he felt that Aina Abdul was the right singer to represent the country at Eurovision.

“Aina is seasoned in major competitions and she knows how to wow both the judges and the audience,” he said. “I am filled with pride.”

Aina Abdul’s inventive wardrobe and her powerful voice sets her apart from the Asian peers, said Adriana Syuhaidah, a fan in Kuala Lumpur.

“She is the Lady Gaga of Malaysia,” she said.
